title: Outlier Pendulum Pedal Review: “What The F*** Are Those?” – Evan Smiley
content:
While the bike industry is in a phase of mostly micro-refinements, Outlier started fresh and totally rethought the flat pedal with the Pendulum. Evan Smiley got ahold of a pair and put them through the wringer to see if this design drops it like it’s hot, or should be relegated to the forgotten corner of the parts bin alongside the HammerSchmidt cranks and pull shocks of yore. Read his review below…

A Curious Design That Really Works, But Not Without Its Quirks.

“What the f*** are those?”

That’s just about the average comment I get when people first see these pedals, and who can blame them? The Outlier Pendulum stands boldly at the end of the cranks. I’ve gotten to know these pedals on 500+ miles across most bikes in my stable. They’ve bounced off rocks in Moab, taken me down steep mountain trails, and spun for miles on the quiet gravel backroads in Vermont. They look sweet, provide a boost in stability and confidence, but have some quirks inherent in their design.

Shape: Stirrups? Weird Brass Knuckles? Useless Spatula?

Top

One of the most standout characteristics of this pedal is its shape. It’s an outer ring with no axle through the middle. All the rigidity and spinning takes place on a stubby axle and two massive inboard bearings. This void allows your shoe to deform into the center hole, making for some serious grip. It also makes a lovely photo frame for trail-side scenery or amphibians. I’d put these in the category of “perfect” grip. Some flat pedals have so many dagger-like pins that once your foot is in place, you can forget about shifting it without a total foot lift. The Pendulum pedals come in a little short of that – and that’s a good thing – with just enough “float” while still locking you in.

One caveat to this category is that I pretty much exclusively ride in Vans. Until they bring back the 5.10 Freerider High, you can pry the floppy vulcanized waffle off my cold dead feet. They’re cheap and they just work. The reason I mention this is so you can take my next complaints with a grain of salt. Recently, on a long bike tour in Vermont, my feet started to get tired when standing and grinding up the steep dirt roads. Sometimes you just have to stand and mash the pedals, whether it’s a crazy steep grade, unweighting your saddle sores, or grinding on a singlespeed. As great as the void in the middle of the pedal was at providing traction, its drawback is that it doesn’t provide much support (duh!). Really, the only time I noticed this was on a tour of long back-to-back days going up and down infinite short, steep hills. Day-to-day riding, this never was a problem, and the pull of the void was nothing but dreamy.

All this said, those who ride on shoes stiffer than a soggy Eggo waffle will probably find this foot fatigue not to be an issue, but theoretically may find their shoe doesn’t quite deflect into the sweet void-pocket as deeply. Even so, the pins are tall enough to lock you in.

You’ll also notice the asymmetric shape about the axle axis. The front of the pedal is a bit wider and matches the ball of your foot just right and tapers as your foot tapers towards the back. This shape is only possible due to the one-sided design of the pedals.

Bottom

Aside from the ever-practical, questionably functional Shimano EH500 hybrid clip pedal and their ilk, I don’t think I’ve ever seen an asymmetric pedal. That is, until you’ve smashed off half the pins on one side of your flats, and then you become intimately familiar with the “good” side. Poor pin maintenance aside, the value of this particular one-sided pedal is not to be understated. Needing not worry about providing any grip for the bottom of the pedals (and there is NONE), Outlier could shape the bottom of the pedal however they wanted, and they sure got it right. The pedal may sit a couple of millimeters closer to the ground compared to a conventional pedal, but their convex shape does wonders at glancing off rocks and roots. I smashed these things more than a few times, and they definitely got hung up less than a traditional pedal on rock strikes. I wouldn’t say I encountered any more rock strikes than other pedals, but I’ll cover that more later. The only consideration I’d impart to Outlier would be to mill in some ridges on the bottom of the pedals on the odd chance you do end up on that side, which is rare, but not uncommon. More on that later as well.

Drop: Drop It Like It’s Hot

Outlier boasts 13 sweet millimeters of drop compared to traditional pedals. It’s like dropping your BB without actually dropping your BB… sort of. Low BBs, so hot right now. Unlike some of the geometry trends that went a little too far in recent years (looking at you, Transition Sentinel V2 and your 63.6 HTA) and are now being brought back from the extremes, it seems like low BBs are here to stay. Despite my grumbling, that seems to be for the best for most riders. I only grumble because I live in the rock mecca of Moab and have shit technique. Bring back the high BB! I digress; we love low BBs! So modern! So stable on descents! The lower the better, right? Well, no. But these pedals bring you down with next to none of the consequences! As mentioned above, at their lowest, these pedals sit just a couple of millimeters below a standard pedal, but I didn’t notice an appreciable increase in rock strikes. So with that concern out of the way, the pros of a lower BB need to be felt to be believed. Goddamn, the stability! If you’ve had the pleasure of riding a mid-2010s MTB and upgrading to a modern full suspension, you know what a game changer modern geometry is, and the stability that a low BB brings is a key constituent of that magic sauce. Instead of riding ON your bike, you are IN your bike. This takes that flavor and cranks it up to 11. Who knew the secret sauce could get even saucier? Lower BB means lower center of gravity, therefore more stability.

So, all this to say, with these pedals you’re effectively dropping your BB without all the consequences of your pedals actually getting closer to the ground. However, as I’ve been alluding to, there are not zero consequences for this drop. The one I encountered on an already low-BBed touring bike was that while the bottom of the pedal isn’t much closer to the ground, your foot sure is. I have men’s size 11 feet. Big, not huge. My toes hang a bit off the front of this pedal, and when standing and putting down the power, my toes found themselves bashing rocks as I pedaled more than usual. This was especially pronounced on my full-suspension bike, where I dove through the travel on some more powerful climbing efforts while standing. Like all changes to your setup, you adapt, but my toes paid the price in the meantime. Do they make steel-toed Vans?

Of course, one way to combat this would be shorter cranks. Ah yes, another excuse to hop on the (waning?) short crank trend! Admittedly, I was running these on 175 mm cranks, so of course I was going to do some toe bashing. If you’ve been eyeing up some of Hope’s 135 mm cranks, perhaps they would pair nicely with these pedals.

Outlier recommends these pedals for shoes size 7 men’s and 8.5 women’s and above. I’d argue that feet much bigger than a size 12M/13.5W may experience an inordinate amount of smashed toes, but your results may vary.

Pendulum

Does your pedal hang low? Does it wobble to the flo’? Pretty much always, yeah.

The only way a performance, one-sided pedal will work is if it “self-rights” every time. It’s always pins-up when you need it. Amazingly, the Outlier Pendulum accomplished this feat, but there are some intrinsic limitations of this design.

First, I’ll start with how Outlier does this. All the mass of the pedal is on the bottom. It wants to be on the bottom. That part is easy. Outlier needed to make sure there was nothing stopping the pedal from getting to its natural state. Outlier needed to defeat FRICTION! I’m actually on my second pair of Pendulum pedals. Outlier made some modifications to their original design since I got the original test pair. From Outlier:

“The original bearings were unsealed to ensure minimal resistance for the self-righting. We have since sourced a custom, fully sealed bearing that provides better protection from the elements while maintaining the low stiction required for the pedal to self-right.

Additionally, we adjusted the weight balance of the Pendulum by slightly lowering the drop and adding more weight to the bottom of the bearing housing. This ensures more consistent performance and helps the pedal find the correct orientation more efficiently without over-rotating.”

These guys are serious. Custom sealed bearings certainly aren’t cheap, and I love to see these minor refinements to perfect the design. Without interference, these pedals are truly where you want them (almost) all the time.

As refined as the design is, I do have to note that there are some inherent limitations, mainly, what happens if the pedals don’t self-right. Well, as mentioned above, you’re on a convex, pin-free, smooth surface 7 mm ABOVE the axle center. It’s tough to keep your feet on the bottom side of these. Luckily, in most scenarios, you just lift your foot for a fraction of a second, the pedal self-rights, and you’re back in business. Not too different from readjusting your foot when you land caddywompus on a traditional flat pedal.

However, a few scenarios have led to these not self-righting. These aren’t entirely rare scenarios. First, I was going down an unfamiliar, steep, backcountry overgrown forest trail; grass and shrubs whipping my legs. I dabbed and went back to the pedal, but ended up on the bottom. A quick lift to allow the pedal to self-right and… I was still on the bottom of the pedal. Hmm. Turns out a piece of grass had wrapped itself around the axle and was preventing the pedal from spinning freely. No biggie, but a situation that folks may find themselves in not infrequently. I’m never sad to have an opportunity to pause and look around, but had this happened on an especially steep, gnarly section, it could have been a doozy!

Another situation I found myself in was a horrifically muddy bike tour on 4×4 and old mining roads around the Dolores River in Colorado. They’d just had some isolated torrential rains. Miles and miles of the classic peanut butter mud and bike-swallowing puddles we’ve all experienced one fateful time or another. Should I have turned around? Yes, but momma didn’t raise no quitter! It would come as no surprise that wheel-stopping mud also stopped the pedals from spinning. Rarely were there any super gnarly descents that made this consequential, and only posed as a small consideration to spin the pedal when getting back on the saddle from pushing. This tour was on V1 of the pedals with the semi-sealed bearings, which Outlier has addressed in the current version. I haven’t had the (mis)fortune of finding myself in axle-deep mud since getting ahold of the current generation pedals, but I imagine the new sealed bearings will handle mud well, while not being totally immune to getting clogged up between the bearing housing and cranks.

So, here are a few scenarios where I found the limitations of a one-sided design. To be clear, these are relatively extenuating situations. The two massive sealed bearings keep spinning in almost all scenarios I’ve been in. For reference, I don’t swap out their pedals if I’m going on a tour/ride where I’m likely to encounter mud; they’re heartier than that. I wouldn’t call these “fair weather” pedals by any means, but just be aware that if you ride in conditions like tall grass or sticky mud frequently, you may be spending a little extra time thinking about your pedals

Geometry: Don’t Call Me A Tweaker

These puppies drop your foot 13 mm, depending on how thick your normal pedals are. Outlier notes users often drop their seat ~12 mm to compensate. So now comes the geometry finagling.

In an ideal world, say you have 12 mm of seatpost exposed; great, drop that seat. Now your bars are 12 mm higher in relation to your saddle. Conveniently, you have 12 mm of spacers under your stem; great! All is right and well with the world; your bike fits basically the same, and you’re just a hair closer to the ground and stable as hell on those descents!

However, sometimes it’s not that easy. Is your seatpost already slammed? Many posts often come with travel-limiting shims to help with that, but not all of them, in which case you’re shopping for a new post. As mentioned earlier, you can also play with shorter cranks. Going from 175 mm to 165 mm cranks makes up most of that ~12 mm while preserving your bar height. What about if you keep your same cranks and drop your seat but your stem is already slammed? Well, you can play with different rise or flipped stems, or shorter-rise bars.

No matter what, you’re in for some tinkering! Nightmarish for some, but if you’re considering these pedals, I have a hunch you’re a bit of an eccentric tinkerer anyway on the eternal hunt for the perfectly fitting bike! Or at least, you love trying out something different. While some will have to make some minor modifications to maintain their current bike fit, one could consider these pedals to be another tool to get your bike feeling *chef’s kiss* just right.

One more note: the two fat bearings sitting next to each other make for a slightly wider Q-factor. While they take up about as much space as a typical pedal sits away from the crank, the bearing shell prevents your foot from floating next to the crank. This is minor, but it always takes a couple miles to get used to when I swap these between bikes.

Final Thoughts

At the end of the day, I think these pedals are neat. I’m a big fan of out-of-the-box designs, especially since modern bikes have become SO refined. Maybe it’s not perfect, and maybe it won’t “revolutionize” pedals as we know them, but Outlier is trying something new. And as far as I can tell, they nearly perfected this idea if you accept the inherent limitations.

Since initially writing this review, Outlier has dropped the Metronome pedal. As they describe it, the Metronome delivers the same performance as the Pendulum, but the platform provides a more conventional pedal feel and accommodates a broader range of shoe sizes. Having not ridden that pedal, I could imagine the foot fatigue I felt being reduced, and I like that it opens up the pedal design to a broader spectrum of feet. It might be worth taking a look if you’d written off the pedals due to either of those factors.

For the Pendulums, I think a few of the quirks of the design are enough to keep them off my daily driver mountain bike – the primary being landing on the bottom of the pedal when doing quick dabs. I love riding at the limit, trying sketchy lines…

Who are these pedals for? They’re for the sure-footed eccentric. The person ready to nerd out at every bike shop or group ride. The tinkerer. The innovation appreciator. They’re not perfect, but they’re fucking cool!

Pros:

  • Lower center of gravity for unmatched DH stability
  • Conversation starter
  • Convex bottom glances off rocks with ease
  • No axle through the platform, allowing for excellent grip
  • Can be used to fine-tune bike fit
  • Beautiful, refined design

Cons:

  • Could throw off your already fine-tuned bike fit
  • Feet get closer to the ground, might catch your toes more frequently
  • Foot fatigue when using less rigid shoes
  • Very insecure when your foot lands on the wrong side of the pedal
